{{about|knot theory|the conjecture in graph theory|Tait's conjecture}}
The '''Tait conjectures''' are three conjectures made by 19th-century mathematician [[Peter Guthrie Tait]] in his [[History of knot theory|study of knots]].<ref name="Lickorish">{{citation
 | last = Lickorish | first = W. B. Raymond
 | authorlink=W. B. R. Lickorish
 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4612-0691-0
 | isbn = 978-0-387-98254-0
 | mr = 1472978
 | page = 47
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag, New York
 | series = Graduate Texts in Mathematics
 | title = An introduction to knot theory
 | volume = 175
 | year = 1997| s2cid = 122824389
 }}.</ref> The Tait conjectures involve concepts in [[knot theory]] such as [[alternating knot]]s, [[chiral knot|chirality]], and [[writhe]]. All of the Tait conjectures have been solved, the most recent being the Flyping conjecture.

==Background==
[[Image:Isthmus.svg|thumb|100px|A reduced diagram is one in which all the isthmi are removed.]]
Tait came up with his conjectures after his attempt to [[knot tabulation|tabulate]] all knots in the late 19th century. As a founder of the field of knot theory, his work lacks a mathematically rigorous framework, and it is unclear whether he intended the conjectures to apply to all knots, or just to [[alternating knot]]s. It turns out that most of them are only true for alternating knots.<ref name="Stoimenow" /> In the Tait conjectures, a knot diagram is called "reduced" if all the "isthmi", or "nugatory crossings" have been removed.

==Crossing number of alternating knots==
Tait conjectured that in certain circumstances, [[crossing number (knot theory)|crossing number]] was a [[knot invariant]], specifically:
<blockquote>Any reduced [[knot diagram|diagram]] of an alternating link has the fewest possible crossings. </blockquote>
In other words, the crossing number of a reduced, alternating link is an invariant of the knot. This conjecture was proved by [[Louis Kauffman]], [[Kunio Murasugi]] (村杉 邦男), and [[Morwen Thistlethwaite]] in 1987, using the [[Jones polynomial]].<ref name="Kauffman">{{cite journal |last1=Kauffman |first1=Louis |authorlink=Louis Kauffman| date=1987 |title=State models and the Jones polynomial |journal=[[Topology (journal)|Topology]] |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=395–407|doi=10.1016/0040-9383(87)90009-7 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
<ref name="MurasugiClassical1">{{cite journal |last1=Murasugi |first1=Kunio |date=1987 |title=Jones polynomials and classical conjectures in knot theory |journal=[[Topology (journal)|Topology]] |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=187–194|doi=10.1016/0040-9383(87)90058-9 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
<ref name="ThistlethwaiteSpanning">{{cite journal |last1=Thistlethwaite |first1=Morwen |authorlink=Morwen Thistlethwaite| date=1987 |title=A spanning tree expansion of the Jones polynomial |journal=Topology |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=297–309|doi=10.1016/0040-9383(87)90003-6 |doi-access=free }}</ref>


==Writhe and chirality==
A second conjecture of Tait:
<blockquote>An amphicheiral (or acheiral) alternating link has zero writhe.</blockquote>
This conjecture was also proved by [[Louis Kauffman|Kauffman]] and [[Morwen Thistlethwaite|Thistlethwaite]].<ref name="Kauffman"/><ref name="ThistlethwaiteWrithe"/>

==Flyping==
[[Image:Flype.svg|thumb|100px|A [[flype]] move.]]
The Tait flyping conjecture can be stated:
<blockquote>Given any two reduced alternating diagrams <math>D_1</math> and <math>D_2</math> of an oriented, prime alternating link: <math>D_1</math> may be transformed to <math>D_2</math> by means of a sequence of certain simple moves called ''[[flype]]s''.<ref name="World">{{MathWorld|TaitsKnotConjectures|Tait's Knot Conjectures}}</ref> </blockquote>
The Tait flyping conjecture was proved by [[Morwen Thistlethwaite|Thistlethwaite]] and [[William Menasco]] in 1991.<ref name="MenascoThistlethwaite">{{cite journal |last1=Menasco |first1=William |authorlink1=William Menasco| last2=Thistlethwaite |first2=Morwen | authorlink2=Morwen Thistlethwaite|date=1993 |title=The Classification of Alternating Links |journal=Annals of Mathematics |volume=138 |issue=1 |pages=113–171|jstor=2946636 |doi=10.2307/2946636 }}</ref>
The Tait flyping conjecture implies some more of Tait's conjectures:
<blockquote>Any two reduced diagrams of the same alternating [[knot (mathematics)|knot]] have the same writhe.</blockquote>
This follows because flyping preserves writhe. This was proved earlier by Murasugi and [[Morwen Thistlethwaite|Thistlethwaite]].<ref name="MurasugiWrithe">{{cite journal |last1=Murasugi |first1=Kunio |date=1987 |title=Jones polynomials and classical conjectures in knot theory. II |journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] |volume=102 |issue=2 |pages=317–318|doi=10.1017/S0305004100067335 |bibcode=1987MPCPS.102..317M |s2cid=16269170 }}</ref><ref name="ThistlethwaiteWrithe">{{cite journal |last1=Thistlethwaite |first1=Morwen |date=1988 |title=Kauffman's polynomial and alternating links |journal=Topology |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=311–318|doi=10.1016/0040-9383(88)90012-2 |doi-access=free }}</ref> It also follows from Greene's work.<ref name="Greene">{{cite journal |last1=Greene |first1=Joshua |date=2017 |title=Alternating links and definite surfaces |journal=Duke Mathematical Journal |volume=166 |issue=11 |pages=2133–2151|bibcode=2015arXiv151106329G |arxiv=1511.06329 |doi=10.1215/00127094-2017-0004 |s2cid=59023367 }}</ref>
For non-alternating knots this conjecture is not true; the [[Perko pair]] is a counterexample.<ref name= "Stoimenow" />
This result also implies the following conjecture:
<blockquote>Alternating amphicheiral knots have even crossing number.<ref name="Stoimenow">{{cite journal |first=Alexander |last=Stoimenow |title=Tait's conjectures and odd amphicheiral knots |journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. |volume=45 |year=2008 |issue=2 |pages=285–291 |arxiv=0704.1941 |citeseerx=10.1.1.312.6024 |doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-08-01196-8 |s2cid=15299750 |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/2008-45-02/S0273-0979-08-01196-8/}}</ref></blockquote>
This follows because a knot's mirror image has opposite writhe. This conjecture is again only true for alternating knots: non-alternating [[chirality (mathematics)|amphichiral]] knot with crossing number 15 exist.<ref>{{MathWorld|AmphichiralKnot|Amphichiral Knot}}</ref>
